draft.title: Narrator and focaliser
card: The narrator is the voice that tells the story. The reader hears the story in this voice.
The focaliser is the character whose eyes the reader sees through. The reader sees events as this character notices and understands them.
The narrator and the focaliser can be different. A narrator using she or he can tell a story that is seen through one character's eyes.
A novel can switch focalisers between chapters. This shows the same events in two ways, because each character notices different things.
draft.remember: The narrator tells the story. The focaliser is the character whose view the reader shares.

a.q: In a novel, what is a focaliser?
opts: The character whose eyes the reader sees events through
The voice that tells the whole story to the reader
The main character who wins at the end of the story
The author who wrote the novel and chose the events
a.why: The focaliser is the character whose view of events the reader shares. The voice that tells the story is the narrator, which is a different job.
a.clue: Think of whose eyes the reader borrows.

b.q: In Chapter 1 of a novel, a storm hits Sam's farm and the story shows Sam's fear for his sheep. In Chapter 2 the same storm is shown through his sister Nina, who is excited by the lightning. What has the author done?
opts: Switched focalisers to show the same events two ways
Changed the narrator from third person to first person
Used a flashback to show events from the past
Added a second storm to make the plot longer
b.why: The storm is the same event, but the reader sees it first through Sam and then through Nina. That is a switch of focaliser. Nothing says the narrator's voice changed to I.
b.clue: Ask whose eyes the reader sees the storm through each time.

a.best: The character whose eyes the reader sees events through

b.best: Switched focalisers to show the same events two ways
